prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, bringing optical timekeeping to the 10^-18 level.
For the discovery of iron-based high-temperature superconductors.

statement.case_for: Both parts are discoveries read directly from nature or measurements pushed to a new regime, which is where I think the prize should sit. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice idea and Ye's record-accuracy realisation gave clocks that agree at the 10^-18 level across independent laboratories, with tests of constants, relativistic geodesy and a coming redefinition of the second. It is the one candidate that most of the committee ranks, with two first places and three top-three placements, and the two-name attribution is clean. Hosono's 2008 observation of superconductivity in doped LaFeAsO was an unexpected experimental surprise that opened a second family of high-Tc materials, was confirmed within weeks and has now stood for eighteen years, with unusually clean single-person credit. Together they are two distinct, mature achievements, and three names total keeps the prize within bounds. I still think the CMB precision mapping (B023) is the most important result on the list for the dark-energy questions I care about, but I am the only one who ranked it, and I should not insist on it against a committee that sees it differently or finds the attribution unmanageable.
statement.case_against: A lattice clock is, to some, an instrument and not a discovery, and the redefinition of the second has not yet happened. Precision timekeeping has been honoured in 2005 (Hall and Hansch) and 2012 (Wineland), so this risks looking like a third helping from the same dish. Hosono's case rests on a discovery whose pairing mechanism is still not understood and which has little technological payoff, and cuprate superconductivity was already recognised. Pairing an atomic-physics clock with a materials discovery is also an arbitrary combination with no common thread, which a purist would call a compromise and not a prize.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock first as a pure measurement advance, with a clean Katori-Ye split, independent reproduction in many national laboratories and an imminent redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I moved toward this view. In my opening I ranked B040 sixth and worried about overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes, but Kroll's argument that the lattice scheme and its 10^-18 systematics control are distinct from comb synthesis and ion clocks is persuasive. I still want to hear from him and Lindroth how they would word the citation so it is not just a second metrology prize, and whether Ludlow, Hinkley and Bloom can be left out without a credit dispute.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the lattice clock first as precision atomic physics at its best, and notes that the Tokyo and JILA efforts reproduced and surpassed each other for two decades, while acknowledging uncertainty about priority and credit for other clock pioneers.
responses.response: I agree on the physics and on the maturity, and her point about independent comparison at the 10^-18 level is what convinces me this is not a one-group claim. Her uncertainty about Lemonde, Gill and others is where I would press: if the committee cannot defend a two-name split against SYRTE, PTB and NPL contributions, the prize loses its clarity. As Secretary I would want the external expert reports to address this directly before we commit.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first because it opened a new observational window, with a firm diffuse flux and source associations, and takes the Halzen-Karle pair as fair and compact despite the large collaboration.
responses.response: I have ranked IceCube third myself and share his enthusiasm for a measurement-led opening of a new window. My difference is about credit: two names for a collaboration of hundreds, with AMANDA and DUMAND precursors outside the slate, is harder to defend than Katori and Ye, and the origin of most of the flux is still open. I keep it as my first alternative and would readily join him if the credit question can be settled.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators first as a conceptual shift with a clean theory-plus-experiment trio, Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, and views the physics as mature and overdue.
responses.response: I place B061 sixth and not higher for the reason that Eriksson himself half-concedes, that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal sits outside the slate, together with partial overlap with the 2016 topological prize. A prize that leaves out the people who proposed the very system in which the effect was observed is contestable. I do not dispute that it is Nobel-worthy; I dispute that this slate of names is the fair way to give it, and I would like him to say how he would handle BHZ.

responses.point: Olsson ranks the Hosono discovery second, stressing that credit is clean, that it was an original experimental discovery and not a refinement, and that the case rests on discovery and not on explanation of the pairing.
responses.response: I share her view and it is why Hosono is in my configuration. Her emphasis on the discovery-not-explanation framing matches the Prize's own wording, and the unresolved mechanism is no reason to wait after eighteen years. Where I am less sure is the rapid Chinese extension to 55 K, which she calls derivative and I would keep in mind for the citation wording so that it credits the discovery of the family and not the Tc record.

uncertainties: Whether B040 and B028 can be defended as two distinct achievements sharing a prize, or whether the committee would prefer a single-part prize.
Whether Katori and Ye can be defended against other lattice-clock contributors, and how strongly the 2005 and 2012 precedents weigh against a third metrology prize.
Whether the unresolved pairing mechanism for iron-based superconductors argues for waiting, and how to treat Kamihara and the early Chinese Tc work in the citation.
How to allocate credit in B023 (WMAP, Planck, Sunyaev, balloon experiments) so that the CMB mapping can be considered seriously at all.
My own recollection of individual roles is unverified and should be checked against the external expert reports.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. My field is string theory and cosmology, so I am closest to the CMB candidate (B023) and may favour it, which is a reason to give less weight to my own first-place ranking there. My supervisor David Gross and my co-author Thomas Van Riet have no connection to any candidate on this shortlist.
